title: 2023 Outlook for Inflation, Cost of Living and Singapore Dollar
what_it_is: 2023 Outlook for Inflation, Cost of Living and Singapore Dollar

sections.label: Singapore 2023 inflation projections
sections.summary: Singapore inflation is expected to stay elevated in the first half of 2023, then slow, with 2023 CPI-All Items projected at 5.5% to 6.5% and MAS Core Inflation at 3.5% to 4.5%.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
sentences.text: Taking these factors into account, inflation in Singapore is expected to remain elevated in the first half of 2023, before slowing more discernibly in the second half, as global inflation moderates and the current tight domestic labour market eases.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
sentences.text: For 2023 as a whole, the CPI-All Items inflation is projected to come in at 5.5% to 6.5%, compared to 6.1% in 2022.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan) (for the Minister for Trade and Industry)
sentences.text: Over the same period, MAS Core Inflation – which excludes accommodation and private transport costs – is expected to average between 3.5% and 4.5%, compared to 4.1% in 2022.

sections.label: MAS pre-emptive monetary tightening
sections.summary: MAS began tightening monetary policy in October 2021, and by end January 2023 the S$NEER had strengthened 7.8% against major trading partners' currencies since then.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: In fact, MAS was very pre-emptive in its response to the pick-up in inflation, having started monetary policy tightening in October 2021, even when global inflationary pressures were relatively modest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: And just to give Members a sense, as at end January 2023, the Singapore dollar nominal effective exchange rate (S$NEER) has strengthened by 7.8% against a basket of currencies of our major trading partners, if you compare that to October 2021, when MAS first began tightening monetary policy.

sections.label: Progressive Wage Credit scheme co-funding
sections.summary: Under the Progressive Wage Credit scheme, the Government is co-funding lower-wage workers' wage increases from 2022 to 2026, with enhanced co-funding shares for 2022 PWCS support.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: For labour costs, the Government is also co-funding the wage increases of lower-wage workers for five years, from 2022 to 2026, under the Progressive Wage Credit scheme (PWCS).

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: As part of this $1.5 billion support package announced in June, the Government's co-funding share of this 2022 PWCS support was enhanced from 50% to 75% for wages up to $2,500, and from 30% to 45% for wages above $2,500 and up to $3,000.

sections.label: Inflation outlook and global uncertainty
sections.summary: CPI-All Items and core inflation are projected higher, but the global market outlook is uncertain due to potential geopolitical tensions and tight supply chains, so a longer-term view is important.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: As I mentioned in my earlier reply, CPI-All Items inflation is projected to be higher, as well as our core inflation, but the global market outlook is uncertain; in part, because of potential geopolitical tensions that we have been seeing in the news almost every day.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: There is also a softening of or normalisation of supply chains but it continues to be tight.

sentences.speaker: Mr Alvin Tan
sentences.text: We are still quite moderate in our expectations for growth, but at the same time, it is important for us to keep a longer-term view.
